name: Vivekanandan KS
title: Nix for SRE: The Zero-drift Hermetic infrastructure for Determinism
abstract:
Nix is a crucial technology for a wide range of domains in IT world, one of the important domains is SRE. In this talk I aim to shift the audience's thinking towards SRE and how we improve the workflow. I'll explain the big loopholes in the current industry standards and explain its hidden technical debt in energy, time, cost etc. I'll quickly introduce Nix and explain how it fits in the SRE domain. I'll explain the mental model of proactive reliability vs passive reliability. I'll also explain why determinism is crucial for SRE. The talk will also give an idea of how Nix + AI + SRE is way better than just using AI + SRE.

In short: Determinism is more important than one might ever think which traditional approaches try their best, but nothing ever came close to what Nix does in the history of tech.

Key takeaways:

- What typical and AI first SRE lacks
- How Nix makes infra easy to predict and gives true determinism
- How Nix provides sovereignty for SRE
- How Nix removes the complexity of DevOps, SRE workflows
- Why it's better to use Nix + AI instead of using AI for SRE etc
- Change in mental model of how u think about the whole SDLC process

Note: Though the topic and description may sound too technical, it actually isn't. It's just a different way of thinking. So this talk is for everyone from beginners to veterans.

name: Suresh Prakash
title: Sharper Skills, Faster Recovery: Authoring AI Skills for Incident Management
abstract: Agent skills are quickly becoming part of how teams respond to incidents. They capture investigation steps, runbook knowledge, and tool usage so that an AI assistant can help during an outage. But a skill that worked well the first time can quietly drift out of date, and a poorly written one can send an agent down the wrong path when every minute counts. This talk looks at the common mistakes teams make when authoring skills for incident management, from treating them as one-off documents to relying on AI where a simple script or a compile-time check would be more reliable. It also covers how to share, review, and maintain skills so they improve after every incident.

name: Balaji Venkatesan
title: A Robot Walks Into Your Kitchen: Hands-on with Reliaburger
abstract:
Your AI agent can already read kubectl output. The trouble is that it was written for human eyes: tables to squint at, exit codes that mean different things in different commands, and log lines that can carry instructions nobody meant it to follow. Hand an agent an admin kubeconfig and you are trusting it to keep promises the cluster never enforces.

[Reliaburger](https://reliaburger.com/) is a container orchestrator in one Rust binary, written by [Miko Pawlikowski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mikolajpawlikowski/) after more than ten years of running platform teams on Kubernetes: scheduler, gossip, Raft, eBPF service discovery, ingress, mTLS, registry, metrics, logs, GitOps and chaos testing, driven by TOML. It is also built for agents from the ground up. `relish agent` answers in one line of JSON that stays within a byte budget, tells the agent which next steps are read-only, wraps everything an app wrote as untrusted, and lets it read the exact source code the cluster runs. An agent never changes the cluster: it proposes, and a person approves.

In this hands-on workshop, Balaji puts it in your hands. Bring a laptop running macOS on Apple silicon or Linux with KVM (Windows is not supported yet) and, if you use one, your favourite coding agent: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and others. You will:

1. Install Reliaburger with one command and start a three-node cluster on your laptop.
2. Deploy an app from a twelve-line TOML file.
3. Wire your agent in with `relish agent setup` (an MCP server, shown as a diff before anything is written) and give it a read-only token that expires.
4. Break things on purpose with the built-in fault injector, then watch your agent find out why with `relish agent context` and `diagnose`, following evidence instead of guessing.
5. Let the agent propose the fix, read the blast radius and the undo command, and approve it yourself. Then write a guardrail policy that lets it roll back small apps on its own, and never delete anything.
6. Tell us what broke, what your agent got wrong and what you would want from an agent-ready platform.

Reliaburger is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and it is version 0.3.2, so it will break. That is the point, and we want to hear about it.

Bring your laptop, your agent and your Kubernetes baggage. Let's see how much of it you need.

name: Neel Shah
title: The Rise of Agentic SRE: Humans, Agents, and Reliability
abstract:
From Reactive to Intelligent: Site Reliability Engineering is Moving Towards Autonomy. As organisations deploy increasingly complex and distributed architectures, traditional methods of incident response based on reactive practices fall behind. The need arises for smarter automation which would allow for quicker detection of anomalies, faster context analysis, and timely interventions within defined constraints. In this sense, agentic SRE is emerging as a discipline in which AI agents learn to analyze telemetry data, establish relationships among various system components, and help SREs with triage, diagnostics, and troubleshooting while respecting certain boundaries.

In this talk, I will discuss the principles of building a robust and dependable platform for agentic SRE, the key components that constitute the architecture, and the observability layer which provides foundational data. I will also examine the necessary safeguards required to ensure autonomy while at the same time keeping operations secure and auditable. Finally, through examples of practical use cases, such as alert triaging, incident copiloting, root cause analysis, and bounded automated remediation, we will explore how AI can be integrated into operations to improve reliability.

name: Manisha Agrawal
title: Implementing Cost-Aware Observability at Scale
abstract:
As observability adoption grows, telemetry grows with it. At enterprise scale, collecting everything “just in case” gets expensive fast, and the bill is only the visible symptom. Cost and signal quality are the same problem, and the cheapest telemetry is the telemetry you never needed.

This session shares practical lessons from operating observability at more than 12 TB of telemetry per day, where small decisions around labels, log verbosity, sampling, ingestion pipelines and retention can have a significant impact on both cost and signal quality. We’ll look at controlling high-cardinality metrics, filtering noisy logs, sampling traces, choosing appropriate retention, and applying controls closer to the source using OpenTelemetry and modern telemetry pipelines.

The technical controls are only half the challenge. How do you convince application teams to accept limits on telemetry they believe they might need someday? We’ll look at the conversations, guardrails, and shared ownership model that helped move the discussion from “the platform is restricting us” to “what telemetry actually provides operational value?”

Cost-aware observability isn’t about collecting less for the sake of saving money. It’s about collecting intentionally, removing noise, preserving the signals that matter, and continuously balancing visibility, reliability, and cost. All this matters even more as AI agents begin to act on this data.

Attendees will leave with practical patterns for building observability systems where every byte has a reason to exist.

name: Muruganandan Jagadesan
title: Technology People Nature
abstract:
Technology. People. Nature.

Finding the Balance to Build a Meaningful Future

Technology inspires me to build.

People inspire me to learn.

Nature inspires me to reflect.

For more than two decades, I have had the privilege of building technology products, leading diverse teams, and exploring emerging technologies.

Along this journey, I have come to realize that meaningful innovation isn't measured by the sophistication of the technology we create, but by the positive impact it brings to people's lives and the world around us.

I've been fortunate to experience all three dimensions — building technology that creates impact, learning with and from people, and discovering the timeless wisdom that nature quietly shares.

The more I reflect, the more parallels I discover between these three worlds.

Technology evolves through principles.

People grow through principles.

Nature thrives through principles.

Yet, in our pursuit of technological advancement, we sometimes overlook the importance of human connection and our relationship with the natural world.

Perhaps the future isn't about choosing one over the other.

It's about finding the right balance between Technology, People, and Nature — harnessing innovation, empowering people, and respecting the world we live in.

Because the future we build should not just be technologically advanced; it should also be human-centered and sustainable.

Welcome to Technology. People. Nature.

name: Vishnusekar Chandrasekaran
title: From Specifications to Reliability: How SDD and AI-DLC Are Reshaping SRE and DevOps
abstract:
The emergence of AI-driven software development is changing how applications are designed, built, tested and operated. Approaches such as Spec-Driven Development (SDD) and Amazon's AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) introduce new opportunities to bring structure, automation and intelligence into the engineering lifecycle. But what does this mean for Site Reliability Engineering and DevOps?

This talk explores how structured specifications can help define reliability requirements, security constraints and operational expectations early in the development process. It examines how AI-assisted workflows can support infrastructure provisioning, CI/CD automation, policy enforcement, testing and operational activities. More importantly, it discusses how SRE and DevOps practices can evolve to establish the guardrails that make AI-driven delivery reliable, secure and production-ready. We will explore the changing responsibilities of engineers, from executing repetitive operational tasks to designing platforms, validating AI-generated outcomes and engineering system reliability. The session concludes with practical perspectives on preparing SRE and DevOps teams for this emerging model of software delivery.

name: Srinivasan Rangachary
title: The Distributed Cache Paradox: When Scaling for Performance Makes Everything Slower
abstract:
Distributed caching is often considered a key enabler of scalability and high performance, but what happens when introducing distributed cache consistency turns a 20-second operation into a 3-minute bottleneck?

Drawing from real-world experience building a multi-tenant Java platform, this talk explores the hidden performance costs of cache invalidation, synchronization, and inter-node communication in distributed architectures. We will examine how different caching strategies-including JVM-local caches, JMS-based invalidation, centralized Valkey/Redis, and clustered caching frameworks—balance performance, consistency, and operational complexity.

Through a practical case study, we will discuss strategies such as batching cache invalidations, reducing messaging overhead, and optimizing bulk operations without compromising data consistency.

Attendees will walk away with actionable insights into identifying caching bottlenecks, understanding architectural trade-offs, and designing more reliable, scalable distributed systems.

name: Rabel Mervin
title: Break It, Then Trace It: Observability for WebAssembly Backends on wasmCloud
abstract:
WebAssembly moved from the browser to the backend - small, sandboxed components that start in milliseconds and run anywhere, including in Kubernetes. But a sandbox is also isolated: how do you see what happened inside, and across several workloads? We start with a request flowing through WebAssembly workloads. Then we turn on OpenTelemetry on webassembly with wasmcloud and break things on purpose.

The talk covers:

- Introduction to WebAssembly and wasmCloud: what a WebAssembly component is, why it's coming to the backend, and how wasmCloud runs it.
- Why a sandbox is hard to observe: what you can and can't see by default.
- Turning on OpenTelemetry: what the host gives you for free, what a component reports itself, and how separate workloads connect into one trace.
- Breaking things on purpose: we introduce real failures, such as slow services and failing calls, and use traces to find exactly where and why they happen.
- Logs and metrics: log lines attached to the right request, and metrics on a dashboard.
- Takeaways: a checklist for making WebAssembly services observable from day one.

You will learn how to capture LLM-specific latency metrics (TTFT and ITL), implement granular FinOps token attribution, stitch distributed traces across agentic tool calls using OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, and enforce real-time safety and PII guardrails without adding hot-path latency. The talk concludes with a live demo showcasing these telemetry pipelines in action on a real-world enterprise environment.

name: Navin Pai
title: Runbooks for the AI SRE Era
abstract:
Your runbook has two readers at 3AM now. The tired human it was written for, and the agent standing next to them. The human fills every gap with judgement. The agent fills it with action. "Restart the service if it looks unhealthy" was a fine instruction for one of them. For the other it's four unanswered questions and a production change.

This talk is what we learnt putting agents in the incident channel and watching them run our runbooks exactly as written, which turned out to be the problem. Three real failure modes: a confidently hallucinated diagnosis, an unsafe action that free reasoning decided was reasonable, and "remove outdated entries" where nobody had ever defined outdated. Every adjective is a landmine.

The fix isn't five hundred lines of YAML. It's making six decisions explicit that a senior engineer already makes in their head: trigger, precondition, verify, stop condition, rollback, and where a human must sit. We'll show the same runbook before and after, the existing schemas you should borrow rather than invent, how to climb from read-only to autonomous one rung at a time, and the part that finally fixes staleness: the agent proposing runbook edits as PRs after every incident, with a human still holding the merge button. The runbook isn't dying. It's being promoted from documentation to interface.

name: Razeen Shaheed
title: Beyond Deployment: Reliability, Security and Uptime in AI-Powered SaaS
abstract:
Building an AI-powered SaaS product is one challenge. Keeping it running reliably after deployment is a completely different story.

While working on AI agents and SaaS platforms, I've realized that getting an application into production is only the beginning. Your servers might be running, your APIs might be responding, and your monitoring dashboard might show everything as healthy. But what happens when an AI agent silently fails to complete a task? Or when a third-party service goes down, a security vulnerability exposes sensitive information, or an unexpected traffic spike affects your entire application?

In this session, I'll explore the challenges of maintaining reliability, security, and uptime in AI-powered SaaS products. We'll look at practical approaches to monitoring, observability, vulnerability management, failure handling, fallback mechanisms, and incident recovery.

I'll also share engineering perspectives from building AI-driven products, including the architectural decisions and trade-offs involved in making these systems more dependable.

Because deploying a product is a milestone. Keeping it secure, available, and reliable is an ongoing responsibility.
bio: I'm Razeen Shaheed, founder of Attunefy and Webverse Arena. I work on building AI agents, automation platforms, and software systems that solve real-world problems. Right now, my focus is on Attunefy, an agentic AI operating system designed to understand conversations, maintain context, and take actions across different applications. I'm particularly interested in AI architecture, system reliability, and the engineering challenges that come with taking AI agents beyond prototypes and making them dependable in the real world.

name: Kunal Das
title: Stop Paying Frontier Prices for Lookup Work
abstract:
AI workloads have landed on the plates of the same teams that already manage compute, storage and network spend, and the default setup is one frontier model for every task. A file lookup costs the same as an architecture decision. The invoice grows, nothing on it says which task needed the big model, and the platform team inherits the bill.

This talk shows the alternative as it runs in an open-source coding agent I use daily. Work is split into roles: a planner decomposes tasks, a builder writes code, a reviewer catches mistakes, and lighter models handle exploration and lookup. Each role goes to the cheapest model that clears its quality bar. Routing decisions are explicit, logged and reversible, and cost is attributed per task, per role and per model from the first day - the same discipline you already apply to every other metered resource.

The failure modes get equal time: the task types where cheap models cost more in rework than they save in tokens, what falls back when a tier fails or a model becomes unavailable, and where the big model still wins. You leave with a way to segment your own inference workloads and the wiring to prove or disprove the savings on your own numbers. All of it is open source.

name: Gayathri G
title: Beyond Traditional Observability: Building Reliable and Observable AI Systems
abstract:
As organizations move from traditional software applications to LLM-powered applications and autonomous AI agents, observability is becoming significantly more complex.

Traditional observability practices built around logs, metrics, and traces are still essential, but they are no longer sufficient to understand the behaviour of AI systems. We also need visibility into LLM interactions, prompt and response quality, agent decisions, tool invocations, token consumption, hallucinations, and multi-agent execution flows.

This session explores the evolving landscape of AI Observability and the engineering practices required to operate AI systems reliably in production.

We will cover:

* Beyond Traditional Observability: How AI observability differs from conventional application monitoring.
* Tracing AI Workflows: Understanding LLM calls, agent execution paths, tool invocations, and multi-agent interactions.
* Performance & Cost Monitoring: Tracking latency, token usage, inference costs, and resource utilization.
* Quality & Reliability: Evaluating responses, detecting hallucinations, monitoring guardrails, and identifying failures.
* Production Readiness: Connecting observability with evaluation, governance, and continuous improvement.

The session aims to provide practical insights into building observable, reliable, and production-ready AI systems, and how SRE principles can evolve to meet the challenges of the agentic AI era.

Her work focuses on taking AI systems from experimentation to production, with an emphasis on AI observability, evaluation, reliability, governance, and performance monitoring. She has worked on building observability capabilities that provide visibility into LLM interactions, agent execution traces, token consumption, latency, costs, decision-making, and response quality.

She is particularly interested in the engineering challenges of operating AI systems reliably at scale and bridging the gap between traditional software observability and the evolving needs of AI-driven applications.

name: Vivek Anandaraman
title: Building an OpenTelemetry Backend with DuckLake: From OTLP to Queryable Telemetry
abstract:
What if you could build an OpenTelemetry backend using DuckLake, DuckDB and object storage, without depending on a traditional observability database?

This talk explores a hands-on engineering project that uses DuckLake as a storage layer for OpenTelemetry logs and metrics. The architecture accepts OTLP JSON payloads through independent ingestion services, buffers incoming data using durable disk-backed queues, and commits telemetry into a shared DuckLake catalog backed by Parquet files on S3-compatible object storage.

We'll explore how the system handles telemetry ingestion, batching, transactional commits, writer recovery, hourly partitioning and Parquet file maintenance. The implementation also exposes a SQL-based query API, allowing Grafana to visualize logs, metrics and even the health of the ingestion pipeline itself.

The session will walk through the architecture, key engineering decisions, trade-offs and lessons learned while building this experimental backend.

Attendees will leave with a practical understanding of how DuckLake and DuckDB can be used to explore alternative storage architectures for OpenTelemetry, and the opportunities and challenges of building an observability lakehouse.
bio: Vivek Anandaraman is the organiser of fromDevtoOps, a Chennai-based community bringing together practitioners in DevOps, SRE, Platform Engineering, cloud, and open source. He is an active open-source contributor and has spoken at KCD Kochi, TOSS Chennai, and SREday, sharing practical insights from operating observability platforms in production and exploring emerging approaches to AI-assisted SRE.

name: Srinivasan Ramanujam
title: Patient Zero: Incident Response for AI Mind Viruses
abstract: Multi-agent systems have a new failure mode: one agent picks up a bad instruction, writes it into its persistent memory, and passes it to every agent it talks to. Recent research from Anthropic and EPFL showed these "mind viruses" surviving context resets across 20 agent hops, carried only by a single prompt file. To an SRE this isn't sci-fi. It's config drift with a replication factor and a cascading failure that never trips a health check. In this talk, I'll infect a small multi-agent system live on stage, then run the incident: how to detect behavioral drift when every request returns 200, how to map blast radius across agent-to-agent messages, how to quarantine and roll back agent memory, and which guardrails actually stop the spread. You'll leave with a practical runbook for running agents in production as untrusted, stateful, self-modifying services.

name: Sahithya Balasubramaniam
title: Who Owns Reliability When AI Agents Make the Decisions?
abstract:
As AI agents become increasingly autonomous, a fundamental question emerges: who is responsible when an AI-driven system fails?

Traditional reliability engineering revolves around predictable services, defined ownership and established incident response practices. Autonomous AI systems challenge these assumptions by introducing dynamic decision-making, multi-agent dependencies, unpredictable execution paths and complex failure scenarios.

This panel explores how engineering teams must rethink reliability in the age of autonomous systems. From accountability in agentic workflows and human oversight to observability, incident ownership, failure recovery and security boundaries, the discussion will examine the evolving relationship between AI autonomy and engineering responsibility.

As organizations move towards increasingly intelligent and interconnected systems, how do we ensure that autonomy does not come at the cost of reliability?

The discussion will bring together diverse engineering perspectives on building, operating and maintaining trustworthy systems in an AI-driven world.

name: Ram Iyengar
title: Cattle, Pets, and Racehorses
abstract:
For over a decade, "treat servers like cattle, not pets" was the north star of Site Reliability Engineering. It taught us to abandon manual heroics in favor of automation, immutability, and graceful failure. Then came AI—and suddenly, we are operating high-density GPU clusters that cannot simply be terminated and replaced. They tend to fail mid-run. You find yourself responsible for multi-terabyte model weights that degrade silently without throwing a 500 error. Autonomous agents built by your teams show unpredictable fan-out which breaks every assumption of traditional capacity planning. Welcome to the era of the Racehorse!

This talk traces the evolution of SRE responsibilities across seven architectural eras—bare-metal, cloud VMs, containers, serverless, AI agents, AI models, and GPU clusters—examining how the hard-won lessons of each generation shaped the next. AI has changed everything and rewritten our playbooks - both literally and figuratively.

We will close with a practical playbook for engineers struggling to define and apply SRE practices to their AI infrastructure today: how to design SLIs and SLOs when system behavior is non-deterministic, where to apply cattle-style automation versus racehorse-style telemetry and checkpointing, and how to build resilient, cost-disciplined AI platforms without reinventing operations from scratch.
